analogy.p: A contact force is like pulling a sledge with a rope: the rope must touch the sledge. A non-contact force is like an invisible elastic band stretching across a gap and pulling things together without touching. This works because the force acts across a gap, through a field. It breaks down because gravity can only pull, whereas a real elastic band can only pull when stretched, and electric and magnetic forces can also push.

bullets: Force = a push or pull on an object caused by an interaction with another object.
Measured in **newtons (N)**; a force of 1 N is about the weight of a small apple (about 100 g) on Earth.
Force is a **vector**: it is drawn as an arrow whose length shows magnitude and whose direction shows direction.
Forces always occur in **interaction pairs**: if object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A (Newton's third law, covered later).
Effects of forces: change shape (stretch, compress, bend), change speed, or change direction of motion.
Forces are measured with a **newtonmeter** (a calibrated spring balance).
All forces are either **contact** or **non-contact**, so be able to place any given force in one of these two groups.
core.p: A **force** is a push or a pull that acts on an object **due to the interaction with another object**. Forces are never 'owned' by one object alone: there are always two objects interacting (for example, your hand and a book, or the Earth and the Moon). The unit of force is the **newton (N)**. Force is a **vector quantity**, so a complete description of a force gives both its size (magnitude) and its direction. Forces can change the speed, direction or shape of an object, and AQA expects you to classify every force as either a contact force or a non-contact force.

bullets: **Scalar**: magnitude only (mass, distance, speed, energy, temperature).
**Vector**: magnitude and direction (force, weight, displacement, velocity, acceleration).
A force arrow is drawn **from the object**, in the direction of the force, labelled with its name (and size in N if known).
Use a scale such as **1 cm = 10 N**: a 30 N force is then an arrow 3 cm long.
Two equal forces in opposite directions have equal-length arrows pointing opposite ways; their resultant is 0 N.
Forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract (the resultant is the difference).
Force is measured in newtons using a newtonmeter; mass is a scalar measured in kilograms using a balance.
Direction words to use: 'downwards', 'upwards', 'towards the centre of the Earth', 'at 90 degrees to the surface', 'opposite to the motion'.
core.h: Vectors, scalars and drawing force arrows
core.p: A **scalar** has size (magnitude) only, such as mass, speed or energy, whereas a **vector** has both size and direction, such as force, weight, velocity and acceleration. Because force is a vector, you must always give a direction as well as a number of newtons, and on a diagram you show it with an arrow. The arrow starts on the object (on the centre of mass for weight), points the way the force acts, and its length is drawn to scale so that a bigger force has a longer arrow. This is why free body diagrams, resultant forces and the correct choice of contact or non-contact force are all linked.

bullets: **Friction**: acts between two surfaces in contact, **opposing** the motion (or attempted motion). It acts parallel to the surfaces and causes heating.
**Air resistance** (drag): friction with air (or fluids such as water) that opposes motion, and increases with speed and surface area.
**Tension**: a pulling force transmitted through a rope, string or cable; it acts along the rope, away from the object.

**Normal contact force**: the push of a surface on an object resting on it, acting at **90 degrees (perpendicular)** to the surface. For an object on a horizontal surface it balances the weight if it is stationary.
Other contact forces: **upthrust** (in fluids), **compression** and **drag**.
A contact force exists only while the objects touch; when contact is lost (e.g. a ball leaving your hand) the force ends.
Contact forces always come with their interaction partner on the other object.
core.p: A **contact force** is a force that acts between two objects that are **physically touching**. At a microscopic level the force comes from electrostatic repulsion between the outer electrons of the atoms at the surfaces, but at GCSE it is enough to say the objects must be in contact. AQA lists friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact force as the standard examples. Each has a definite direction, which is important when drawing free body diagrams and finding resultant forces.

bullets: **Gravitational force**: an attractive force between any two objects with mass. It is only noticeable when at least one object is very massive (e.g. a planet).
**Electrostatic force**: acts between charged objects; like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
**Magnetic force**: acts between magnets, and between magnets and magnetic materials (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel). Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
Non-contact forces act through a **field** (gravitational field, electric field, magnetic field).
The strength of the force decreases as the separation increases.
Example: a falling ball is pulled to the Earth by gravity before it touches the ground; no contact is needed.
Contact versus non-contact: always check whether the two objects are touching; this is the test.
Gravitational forces are always attractive; electrostatic and magnetic forces can be attractive or repulsive.
core.p: A **non-contact force** is a force that acts between objects **without them touching**. It acts across a gap through a **field**, which is the region around an object where another object feels a force. AQA names three: **gravitational force**, **electrostatic force** and **magnetic force**. They are all felt over a distance, they get weaker as the distance increases, and each one is associated with a different property of the objects involved (mass, electric charge, or magnetism).

bullets: Gravity always **attracts**; it never repels.
Gravitational field strength g = force on 1 kg of mass, in **N/kg**, and it acts towards the centre of the planet.
On Earth g = **9.8 N/kg**; on the Moon g = about **1.6 N/kg**; on Jupiter g is about 25 N/kg.
The field is stronger closer to a planet and weaker further away, so g decreases as you move away from the Earth.
The bigger the mass of the planet, the stronger its field at the surface.
Near the Earth's surface the field is approximately uniform (the same everywhere nearby).
Gravity keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth and planets in orbit around the Sun, and it is why objects fall.
core.p: **Gravity** is the attractive force between all objects that have mass. Near the Earth, the force of gravity on an object is due to the **gravitational field** around the Earth. A gravitational field is the region where a mass experiences a force because of another mass. The strength of the field at a point is the **gravitational field strength (g)**, measured in **newtons per kilogram (N/kg)**: it tells you the force on each kilogram of mass placed at that point. Close to the surface of the Earth g is about **9.8 N/kg** (often rounded to 10 N/kg, but use the value given in the question).

bullets: **W = m g** (weight in N = mass in kg x gravitational field strength in N/kg).
Rearrangements: **m = W / g** and **g = W / m**.
Weight is measured using a **calibrated spring balance (newtonmeter)**.
Weight acts downwards, towards the centre of the Earth, and is shown as an arrow starting at the centre of mass.
If the unit of mass is grams, convert to kilograms before using the equation (divide by 1000).
Weight is a **force** (vector); you should never say an object has a 'weight in kg'.
A 1 kg mass has a weight of 9.8 N on Earth but only 1.6 N on the Moon.
Astronauts feel 'weightless' in orbit because they and the spacecraft are in free fall together, not because gravity has disappeared.
core.h: Weight and the equation W = m g
core.p: **Weight** is the force acting on an object due to gravity. It is a force, so it is measured in **newtons**, and it is a vector acting **vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth**. The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is, so the same object has different weights on different planets. The relationship is **weight = mass x gravitational field strength**, written W = m g, where W is weight in newtons (N), m is mass in kilograms (kg) and g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). You must be able to use and rearrange this equation.

bullets: Mass: scalar, kg, constant everywhere, measured with a balance.
Weight: vector (force), N, depends on g, measured with a newtonmeter/spring balance.
**Weight is directly proportional to mass**: W is proportional to m, with constant of proportionality g.
A graph of weight against mass is a **straight line through the origin**; its **gradient = g** (in N/kg).
An astronaut of mass 70 kg has the same mass on the Moon, but their weight is about 6 times smaller there (1.6 compared to 9.8).
In deep space, far from any mass, weight is close to zero but mass is unchanged.
Comparison sentence for the exam: 'Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same; weight is the force of gravity on the object and depends on the gravitational field strength.'
core.p: Students often mix up mass and weight, and examiners test it constantly. **Mass** is the amount of matter in an object; it is a scalar measured in kilograms and does not change with location. **Weight** is the gravitational force on that mass, a vector measured in newtons, and it changes with the strength of the gravitational field. Mass is measured with a balance, weight with a newtonmeter. The two are linked because **weight is directly proportional to mass**: doubling the mass doubles the weight (at the same g).

bullets: Approximate values: **Moon 1.6 N/kg, Mars 3.7 N/kg, Earth 9.8 N/kg, Jupiter about 25 N/kg**.
Weight on the Moon is about **one sixth** of the weight on Earth for the same object (1.6 / 9.8 is about 0.16).
A 60 kg person has a weight of 60 x 3.7 = **222 N** on Mars and 60 x 9.8 = **588 N** on Earth, but a mass of 60 kg on both.
If a question gives weight and mass, g = W / m; the answer in N/kg identifies the planet.
Higher g means a larger force on each kilogram, so objects fall with a greater acceleration (free fall acceleration is numerically equal to g in m/s squared).
Far from every planet or star the gravitational field is very weak, so the weight is close to 0 N, but the mass is unchanged.
Always state both the mass (kg) and the weight (N) in comparison answers, with units.
core.h: Gravitational field strength on other bodies
core.p: The same mass has a different weight on each planet or moon because each body has its own gravitational field strength g. A body with a larger mass (and smaller radius) has a stronger field at its surface. Because W = m g and the mass of an object does not change, you can compare weights simply by comparing the values of g. Questions usually give the value of g, so read the data carefully and always keep the unit N/kg. This is the cleanest way to show the examiner that you understand mass and weight are different quantities.

bullets: The **centre of mass** is the single point at which the weight of an object may be considered to act.
For a uniform regular object it is at the geometric centre.
Weight arrow: drawn from the centre of mass, vertically downwards.
An object balanced at its centre of mass will not rotate, since there is no turning effect from its weight about that point.
The lower the centre of mass and the wider the base, the more stable an object is.

Finding the centre of mass of an irregular lamina: hang it freely from a pin at one hole, hang a plumb line from the pin and mark it; repeat from a second hole; the centre of mass is where the lines cross.
The centre of mass need not lie inside the object (e.g. a ring).
core.p: The weight of an object is spread through the whole object, since every particle is pulled by gravity. For calculations and diagrams, the weight can be **considered to act at a single point, called the centre of mass**. For a uniform, symmetrical object (such as a metre ruler, sphere or cube) the centre of mass is at the geometrical centre. For irregular objects it can be found by suspending the object from different points and drawing vertical plumb lines. This idea means a free body diagram can show weight as one arrow, drawn from the centre of mass downwards.

bullets: **Method**: hang a newtonmeter from a clamp stand; add 100 g (0.1 kg) masses one at a time; record the force reading each time.
**Independent variable**: mass (kg). **Dependent variable**: weight (N). **Control**: use the same newtonmeter, same location (same g).
Check the newtonmeter reads 0 N before adding masses (zero error); read the scale at eye level to avoid **parallax error**.
Convert grams to kilograms before plotting.
Plot weight (y-axis) against mass (x-axis); draw a **line of best fit** through the origin.
**Gradient** = change in weight / change in mass = g; expected about 9.8 N/kg.
A straight line through the origin shows the quantities are **directly proportional**.
Spread of points above/below the line indicates random error; a line that does not pass through the origin suggests a systematic (zero) error.
core.h: Investigating the link between mass and weight
core.p: A standard classroom investigation checks that weight is proportional to mass. Masses are added in steps to a newtonmeter and the weight is read each time. Plotting the results gives a straight line through the origin, and the gradient gives g. The investigation is not on AQA's list of required practicals but it is a very common data question and it practises graph skills. The reasoning behind it matters: the experiment confirms proportionality because the line is straight and passes through (0, 0).

bullets: A **free body diagram** shows all the forces acting on a single object and nothing else.
Weight is a non-contact force, drawn downwards from the centre of mass.
Normal contact force is perpendicular to the surface, upwards on a horizontal surface.
If weight = normal contact force, the forces are **balanced** and the resultant force is 0 N (no vertical acceleration).
A falling object near Earth: weight (down) is greater than air resistance (up), so there is a resultant force downwards and the object accelerates.
At terminal velocity weight = air resistance, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity is constant.
The arrow lengths should reflect the sizes of the forces.
In a lift or when pushing off the ground, the normal contact force can be larger or smaller than the weight, explaining why you feel heavier or lighter.
core.h: Resultant forces, balanced forces and free body diagrams
core.p: When an object is at rest on a surface, the weight acting downwards is balanced by the normal contact force acting upwards, so the resultant force is zero. In free body diagrams, every force on one object is drawn as an arrow from the centre of the object, labelled with its name and size where known. Weight (non-contact) and the contact forces are shown together, which is why this topic links so tightly with 'contact versus non-contact'. The resultant force is the vector sum of all these forces.

bullets: Newton's third law: when two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
Pair forces act on **different** objects so they never cancel.
The pair of the Earth's pull on a book (weight) is the book's pull on the Earth (both gravitational).
The pair of the normal contact force of the table on a book is the force of the book on the table.
Weight and normal contact force on a stationary book are **not** a third law pair: same object, different types.
Pair forces are always the same type (gravitational with gravitational, contact with contact).
When you step off a boat, you push the boat backwards (contact pair).
core.h: Interaction pairs and Newton's third law (link)
core.p: Every force comes with an equal and opposite partner force acting on a different object. For example, the Earth pulls you down with a gravitational force (your weight); you pull the Earth up with an equal gravitational force. The pair forces are of the same type, have the same magnitude, act in opposite directions and act on different objects, which is why they do not cancel each other out. This is a common trap: weight and normal contact force on a book are not an interaction pair, they act on the same object and are different types of force.

bullets: **Gravitational potential energy**: E_p = m g h (J); g = 9.8 N/kg is used again.
**Orbits**: gravity provides the force towards the centre, changing velocity but not speed for a circular orbit.
**Terminal velocity**: compare weight and air resistance.
**Static electricity** (Physics Paper 1): electrostatic forces are non-contact forces between charged objects.
**Magnetism** (Paper 2): force between magnets is non-contact; field lines show direction.
**Higher tier**: weight can be resolved into components along and perpendicular to a slope.
On a slope, the component of weight down the slope = W sin(angle), and perpendicular = W cos(angle) (resolving forces; may appear in Higher questions).
Comparing planets: the greater g on Jupiter means the same mass has a bigger weight there than on Earth.
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Gravity and weight are connected to many other parts of the specification. Gravitational potential energy depends on weight: E_p = m g h, where g is the gravitational field strength. Orbital motion (Space physics) uses gravity as the force that keeps satellites in orbit. Non-contact electrostatic forces are the basis of static electricity and electrostatic effects on charge, while magnetic forces link to magnetism and electromagnetism. Finally, the effect of friction and air resistance leads into terminal velocity. Being clear on the types of forces helps you answer questions across Paper 2.

exam: **Classify forces (1-3 marks)**: contact = friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force; non-contact = gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic. Say whether the objects touch.
**Define weight (1 mark)**: 'The force acting on an object due to gravity.' Do not say 'how heavy it is'.
**Calculation (2-3 marks)**: write W = m g, substitute with correct units (kg, N/kg), give the answer in N. Show the rearranged form for m or g.
**Mass vs weight (2-4 marks)**: mass = amount of matter (kg, same everywhere, scalar); weight = force of gravity (N, depends on g, vector). Include both a definition and a unit for full marks.
**'Explain why weight changes on the Moon' (2 marks)**: the Moon has a weaker gravitational field strength (1.6 N/kg); weight = mass x g, so weight is smaller, but mass is unchanged.
**Direction**: always state that weight acts downwards/towards the centre of the Earth; normal contact force at 90 degrees to the surface.
**Free body diagrams**: arrows from the centre, correct directions, lengths in proportion, labelled. Balanced forces mean equal lengths.
**Graph questions**: weight against mass is a straight line through the origin; gradient = g; 'directly proportional' needs both words 'straight line' and 'through the origin'.
**Experiment (required language)**: independent variable mass, dependent variable weight, control same newtonmeter and location; read at eye level.
**Command words**: 'State' brief answer; 'Describe' what happens; 'Explain' because/so; 'Calculate' with working.
**Common mark loss**: no units, no conversion to kg, or mixing up mass and weight.
**Planet comparison (2-3 marks)**: same mass on each body, so the weight is proportional to g; the body with the larger g gives the larger weight. Give numbers with units.

mistakes.r: Weight is a force measured in newtons (N). Mass is measured in kilograms.
Mass stays the same everywhere; only the weight changes because g is different (1.6 N/kg on the Moon).
Gravity acts everywhere but gets weaker as distance from the mass increases.
mistakes.w: Gravity does not exist in space or at the top of a mountain.

mistakes.r: They act on the same object and are different types of force. The pair of weight is the object's gravitational pull on the Earth.
mistakes.w: Weight and the normal contact force are an action-reaction pair.

mistakes.r: Use the value of g given in the question. If none is given, use 9.8 N/kg unless told otherwise.
mistakes.w: Using g = 10 when the question says 9.8 (or the reverse).

mistakes.r: Magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces are non-contact forces acting through fields.
mistakes.w: Magnetic forces need contact to work.

mistakes.r: Weight acts from the centre of mass, vertically downwards.
mistakes.w: Weight acts from the point where the object touches the ground.

mistakes.r: Convert first: 250 g = 0.25 kg. Then W = 0.25 x 9.8 = 2.45 N.
mistakes.w: Not converting grams to kilograms in W = m g.

mistakes.r: Friction opposes the motion or attempted motion between surfaces. It can be the force that makes you move forward when you walk.
Weight acts from the centre of mass, towards the centre of the Earth (vertically downwards).
mistakes.w: Saying gravity acts 'down' with no reference point, or saying weight acts at the floor.

summary: The specification asks you to classify forces as contact (friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force) or non-contact (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic), and to understand that weight is the force of gravity on a mass, calculated with W = m g, acting at the centre of mass. It matters because every free body diagram, resultant force and energy calculation depends on recognising these forces and using weight correctly. It also expects you to know that weight and mass are directly proportional (the gradient of a weight-mass graph is g), that weight is measured with a calibrated newtonmeter, and to find a centre of mass experimentally.

terms.d: A push or pull on an object due to its interaction with another object; a vector measured in newtons.
A force that acts between objects that are physically touching.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, through a field.
A contact force between two surfaces that opposes motion or attempted motion.
The frictional force from air (a fluid) that opposes the motion of an object moving through it.
A pulling force transmitted through a rope, string or cable.
The force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it, acting at right angles to the surface.
The attractive non-contact force between objects with mass.
A non-contact force between charged objects: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
A non-contact force between magnets or between a magnet and a magnetic material.
A region in which an object experiences a non-contact force, e.g. gravitational, electric or magnetic.
The force per unit mass at a point in a gravitational field, in N/kg (9.8 N/kg on Earth).
The force acting on an object due to gravity; W = m g, measured in newtons.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; it does not change with location.
The single point at which the weight of an object may be considered to act.
A calibrated spring balance used to measure force (and weight) in newtons.
Two quantities where doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction, such as force or weight.
A quantity that has magnitude only, such as mass, speed or energy.
A string with a weight on the end that hangs vertically; used to find the centre of mass of a lamina.

worked.ans: Weight on Earth = 686 N; weight on the Moon = 112 N (mass stays 70 kg).
worked.q: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg on Earth and 1.6 N/kg on the Moon. Calculate the astronaut's weight on each. (4 marks)
steps: Mass is unchanged at 70 kg on both.

worked.ans: Mass = 5.0 kg; weight on the Moon = 8.0 N.
worked.q: A rock has a weight of 49 N on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate its mass, and its weight on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). (4 marks)
steps: Rearrange W = m g to m = W / g.
Weight on the Moon = m g = 5.0 x 1.6 = 8.0 N.

worked.ans: Weight is directly proportional to mass; gradient = 9.8 N/kg = g on Earth.
worked.q: Masses of 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 kg have weights of 0.98, 1.96, 2.94 and 3.92 N. Describe the relationship and calculate the gradient. (3 marks)
steps: The graph of weight against mass is a straight line through the origin, so weight is directly proportional to mass.
Gradient = change in weight / change in mass = 3.92 / 0.4 = 9.8.
Units: N/kg, so the gradient equals the gravitational field strength g.
